topics.title: Global Liveability Index 2026
bullets: The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) released the Global Liveability Index 2026 on 8 July 2026.
It ranked 173 cities worldwide on quality of life parameters.
Copenhagen, Denmark, retained the top spot for the second consecutive year, scoring a near-perfect 98 out of 100 . What is the Global Liveability Index? –
The Global Liveability Index is an annual city ranking published by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) , a research and analysis division of The Economist Group.
It assesses which cities around the world offer the best and worst living conditions based on 30 qualitative and quantitative indicators.
The current methodology and expanded city coverage have been in place since around 2013.

The Global Liveability Index evaluates cities using 30 qualitative and quantitative indicators grouped into five categories: ➢Stability (25%), ➢Culture and Environment (25%), ➢Infrastructure (20%), ➢Healthcare (20%), ➢Education (10%).
Each indicator is rated as acceptable, tolerable, uncomfortable, undesirable, or intolerable, and these ratings are weighted to provide a score from 1 to 100.
The overall livability score is a weighted aggregate of these five categories.
The 2026 edition of the index assessed 173 cities. Key Facts –
Copenhagen, Denmark, has been named the world's most liveable city for the second consecutive year with a score of 98 out of 100.
The Danish capital earned perfect scores (100 out of 100) in stability, infrastructure, and education.
It also scored 96 in healthcare and 95 in culture and environment, reflecting its people-first approach to urban living.
Vienna, Austria, secured the second position with an overall score of 97 out of 100.
Vienna earned perfect scores (100) in healthcare, infrastructure, and education, and scored 95 in stability and 94 in culture and environment.
Vienna held the top spot for multiple consecutive years (2022-2024), while Copenhagen took the number one position in 2025 and 2026.
Melbourne, Australia, ranked third globally, rising one spot from the previous year.
Melbourne shines on account of its world-class healthcare and impressive education – scoring 100 in both categories.
Australia made a strong showing, with Sydney (4th), Adelaide (8th), and Melbourne all featuring in the global top 10.
The top 10 cities in the 2026 index are: 1. Copenhagen, 2. Vienna, 3. Melbourne, 4. Sydney, 5. Zurich, 6. Geneva, 7. Osaka, 8. Adelaide, 9. Vancouver, 10. Tokyo.
Western Europe remains the strongest region, with Copenhagen, Vienna, Zurich, and Geneva all featuring in the top six.
Australia secured three spots, while Canada (Vancouver) and Japan (Osaka, Tokyo) also feature prominently.
While Western Europe's average score has stagnated, Asia's has been rising steadily – by 0.3 points to 73.9 in 2026.
Damascus, Syria, remained the world's least liveable city for the second consecutive year.
Tehran entered the bottom 10 this year, marking a fresh low for the Iranian capital. Indian Cities Performance –
New Delhi ranked 120th out of 173 cities with an overall score of 48.1.
Delhi's category-wise scores were: education (66.7), infrastructure (58.9), stability (50), healthcare (41.7), and culture and environment (35.4).
Mumbai ranked 121st with an overall score of 47.9.
Chennai ranked 123rd in the 2026 index.
Bengaluru ranked 127th, the lowest among the four Indian cities assessed.
Neither New Delhi nor Mumbai saw any movement in their rankings compared to the previous year. EIU –
The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) is the research and analysis division of The Economist Group, the British media company that publishes The Economist newspaper.
It was founded in 1946 specifically to address the questions that readers of The Economist were asking and to provide business intelligence to both the newspaper and external clients.
Today, the EIU provides forecasting and advisory services through research and analysis, including monthly country reports, five-year economic forecasts, and country risk service reports.
EIU was created in 1946 to help businesses, financial firms, and governments understand how the world is changing and how to manage risks and seize opportunities.
In 1987, the EIU acquired Business International Corporation, a UK company that significantly expanded its global research capabilities.

Key acquisitions over the years have strengthened its expertise in specialized areas, including healthcare (Clearstate in 2012, Bazian in 2012), telecommunications (Pyramid Research in 1997), and consumer analytics (Canback & Company in 2015).
The EIU is an independent business unit within The Economist Group, headquartered in London, England.
It has main offices in four cities – London, New York, Hong Kong, and Dubai.
The Managing Director of the EIU is Leon Calvert, who was appointed in April 2025.

topics.title: TN asks EC to Step Down
bullets: The Tamil Nadu government led by Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay has asked State Election Commissioner B. Jothi Nirmalasamy to step down from her post.
Nirmalasamy, a retired IAS officer, assumed office in March 2024 for a five-year term that was to end in May 2029.
The move comes amid a series of resignations of officials appointed by the previous DMK government, raising questions about the constitutional protection enjoyed by the office. Background –
The State Election Commission (SEC) is a constitutional and autonomous body responsible for conducting free and fair elections to local self-governments.
It was established under the provisions of the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments Acts of 1992.
The Commission is responsible for the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Panchayats and Urban Local Bodies.
Article 243K of the Constitution of India provides for the establishment of a State Election Commission consisting of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor.
The superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to the Panchayats shall be vested in the Commission.
Similar provisions for Urban Local Bodies are contained in Article 243ZA of the Constitution.
The Tamil Nadu State Election Commission was formed on 15 July 1994.
It is an autonomous, independent Constitutional and Statutory authority of Tamil Nadu.
All Local Body elections of Tamil Nadu are conducted by this Commission.
The State Election Commissioner shall hold office for a term not exceeding five years from the date on which they enter upon their office.
They are not eligible for re-appointment. 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments –
The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions.
It added Part IX to the Constitution, containing Articles 243 to 243O.
The Amendment provided for the establishment of a State Election Commission in every State to conduct elections to the Panchayats.
The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies.
It added Part IXA to the Constitution, containing Articles 243P to 243ZG.
The Amendment provided for the establishment of a State Election Commission to conduct elections to the Municipalities.
These amendments were designed to strengthen democracy at the grassroots level.
They created a three-tier system of local self-governance.
The establishment of the State Election Commission was a crucial step to ensure that local body elections are conducted in a free and fair manner.
The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor of the State.
The Supreme Court has held that State Election Commissioners must be independent persons who cannot be persons occupying a post or office under the Central or any State Government.
The appointment must be made in accordance with the constitutional mandate to ensure the independence of the office.
The conditions of service of the State Election Commissioner cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment.
This protection ensures that the Commissioner is not subject to retaliatory action by the government.
The conditions of service are subject to the provisions of any law made by the State Legislature.
The Commission has the power to superintend, direct, and control the conduct of all elections to local bodies.
It prepares the electoral rolls for local body elections.
It can also tender opinions to the government on matters relating to elections. Legal Framework –
Article 243K(2) provides that the State Election Commissioner shall not be removed from office except in the like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of a High Court.
This provision is designed to ensure the independence of the State Election Commission.
Any attempt to remove the Commissioner without following this procedure would be unconstitutional.
A High Court Judge can be removed only on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
The removal requires an address by both Houses of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
The same stringent procedure applies to the removal of a State Election Commissioner. Jothi Nirmalasamy Controversy –
B. Jothi Nirmalasamy is a retired IAS officer of the 1992 batch.
She assumed office as the State Election Commissioner in March 2024 for a five-year term.

She is the only IAS officer to have received the state government's Kalpana Chawla Award for courage and daring enterprise, awarded in 2008 for her action against the sand mafia in Kanyakumari district.
Nirmalasamy was appointed by the previous DMK government, succeeding retired IAS officer V. Palanikumar.
Her tenure was for five years or until she attained 65 years of age, whichever was earlier.
She is also the Chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Delimitation Commission.
As Chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Delimitation Commission, Nirmalasamy has been overseeing the sanctioning and mapping of wards.
She has been overseeing delimitation work in 27 districts, including four municipal corporations, 12 municipal councils, and several rural panchayats.
The delimitation process is a key prerequisite for holding local body elections.
Nirmalasamy has been overseeing the phased introduction of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) for rural local body elections.
The Commission has procured around 50,000 EVMs from BHEL for the rollout, enabling voters to cast four votes electronically.
She also oversaw the indirect by-elections to several urban local bodies following the resignation of mayors.
The tenure of rural local bodies in 28 districts ended on January 25, 2025.
The tenure of local bodies in the remaining nine districts will end on October 19, 2026.
The tenure of all urban local bodies is scheduled to end on March 1, 2027. The Recent News –
On July 8, 2026, it was reported that the Tamil Nadu government had asked State Election Commissioner B. Jothi Nirmalasamy to step down.
The request came ahead of the local body elections.
Nirmalasamy has not taken a decision on the matter as yet.
The move comes after the government asked chairpersons and members of several other state bodies to step down.
Former Chief Secretary Shiv Das Meena resigned as chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority (TNRERA).
Former DGP Shankar Jiwal resigned as chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Fire Commission.
Critics have accused the C. Joseph Vijay government of seeking to purge institution heads appointed by the previous DMK government.
The government is reportedly seeking to replace officials appointed by the previous administration. The move has been criticised as an attempt to undermine the independence of constitutional bodies.

According to reports, Nirmalasamy seems interested in continuing to complete the work she has initiated for the local body elections. Passage: The Election Commission of India remained at the centre of national attention during the 2026 election cycle, when Assembly elections were conducted across several politically significant states and a Union Territory. The electoral exercise involved the deployment of polling personnel, electronic voting machines, security forces and observers across thousands of constituencies. The elections were accompanied by debates over electoral-roll accuracy, Special Intensive Revision exercises, voter exclusions and the neutrality of election authorities. West Bengal witnessed particularly intense scrutiny following large- scale changes to its electoral rolls before polling. The Commission maintained that revision exercises were intended to remove deceased, duplicate and otherwise ineligible entries, while critics alleged that eligible voters could also be affected. Source: Indian Express
